text: Not every matrix is equally hard to work with. Identity, diagonal, and block-diagonal matrices show up constantly in quantum computing because they're cheap to compute with and map onto real physical structure.

The identity matrix I has 1's down the diagonal and 0's everywhere else, and its defining property is that I times M equals M times I equals M — as a transformation, it's the 'do nothing' gate. A diagonal matrix has nonzero entries only on its diagonal, and multiplying by one is much cheaper than a general matrix multiplication.

Take D equals 3,0,0, negative 2 and M equals 1,2,3,4. D times M scales each row of M by D's matching diagonal entry, giving 3,6, negative 6, negative 8 — no dot products needed. Multiply in the other order, M times D, and it scales columns instead, giving 3, negative 4,9, negative 8. The two results are still different from each other.

A block-diagonal matrix is built from smaller blocks placed along the diagonal with zeros elsewhere. Take two 2 by 2 blocks and apply the combined 4 by 4 matrix to the vector 1,1,1,0: the top two entries of the result come only from the first block acting on the top half of the vector, and the bottom two entries come only from the second block acting on the bottom half. The blocks never mix — exactly the structure you need when two qubits evolve independently of each other.
